notes.meaning: The story opens by introducing Kish, a wealthy and influential man from the tribe of Benjamin. His family line is traced back several generations, showing that he came from an established and honorable family in Israel. Even though Benjamin was the smallest tribe, Kish had standing, wealth, and strength.

Kish has a son named Saul, who is strikingly handsome and stands a head taller than anyone else in the nation. He looked like the perfect king that the people had been clamoring for, someone impressive and strong who could lead them in battle. Yet the text noticeably mentions nothing about his faith or spiritual life at this stage, only his outward appearance.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Saul is the only Israelite in the Old Testament whose impressive height is singled out, mirroring how the Bible usually describes intimidating foreign enemies rather than Israelite heroes.

notes.meaning: Some valuable donkeys belonging to Kish wander away, so he sends Saul and a servant to track them down. In those days, donkeys were costly work animals and mounts for important people, making this a serious errand. God used this ordinary, frustrating household problem to guide Saul straight to his destiny.

Saul and his servant travel extensively through the hill country of Ephraim and several nearby districts, but find no trace of the animals. Saul shows great diligence and persistence by pressing on through rough terrain instead of giving up quickly. Yet every dead end was quietly steering them along the path God intended.

When they reach the district of Zuph, Saul suggests turning back so his father will not stop worrying about the lost donkeys and start worrying about them. This thoughtful concern shows that Saul was a dutiful, caring son who respected his father's feelings. At the very moment Saul is ready to quit, he arrives right at the outskirts of Samuel's hometown.

The servant points out that a respected man of God lives in the nearby town whose prophecies never fail. He suggests asking this prophet for direction to find the missing donkeys. While the servant shows great respect for Samuel's reliable reputation, both men view the prophet more as a finder of lost property than as God's spiritual guide for the nation.

Saul hesitates because their travel provisions are gone and they have no gift to present to the prophet. In ancient Eastern culture, approaching an important leader or man of God without a polite gift was seen as a lack of basic respect. Saul was not trying to buy a revelation, but simply observing proper manners toward an honorable elder.

The servant discovers that he has a small piece of silver, a quarter of a shekel, which he gladly offers to give to the prophet. This was a modest amount, intended as a courtesy token rather than a fee. The servant's generous willingness allows them to move forward with the visit.

The narrator adds a brief historical note explaining that in earlier times, a prophet was called a seer. The word seer highlighted someone given spiritual insight by God to see things hidden from ordinary eyes. Over time, the term prophet became the standard word for someone who speaks God's message to the people.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Scholars generally regard this parenthetical explanation as a note added by a later compiler to explain an archaic term to later readers.

notes.meaning: Saul approves of the servant's idea and agrees to visit the prophet, so they set off toward the town. Saul's willingness to listen to his servant reveals an approachable, humble attitude at this point in his life. God used the servant's initiative to bring the future king directly to Samuel.

As they climb the hill leading up to the town, they meet young women heading outside the walls to draw water from the spring. Saul asks them whether the seer is currently in the town. Going out for water was a daily routine for young women, and meeting them at the well became the providential key to finding Samuel without delay.

The young women answer eagerly that the seer is just ahead of them and has arrived in town that very day. A public sacrifice and religious feast were scheduled on the high place, which was an outdoor altar built on an elevation near the town. Their detailed answer shows that Samuel's presence was a well-known, celebrated event in the community.

The maidens urge them to hurry into the town before Samuel goes up to the high place to feast. They explain that the guests will not begin eating until Samuel arrives to ask God's blessing on the sacrifice. This practice shows the deep respect the community had for Samuel's priestly role and reflects the ancient roots of giving thanks before meals.

Saul and his servant walk up into the town, and just as they enter, Samuel himself is coming toward them on his way to the high place. The timing of their meeting was precise down to the minute. Though Samuel was the leading figure in Israel, he moved among the people without royal pomp or bodyguards.

The narrative steps back to explain that the Lord had privately spoken to Samuel the day before Saul arrived. In the Hebrew expression, God had uncovered Samuel's ear, like someone whispering an important secret. God had already prepared the prophet so that Saul's arrival would not catch him by surprise.

God tells Samuel that He will send a man from Benjamin to be anointed as the leader over Israel to rescue them from Philistine oppression. Even though the people had shown a lack of trust by demanding a human king, God in His mercy still heard their distressed cries. Anointing with olive oil meant setting someone apart for a special, sacred office under God's authority.

When Samuel lays eyes on Saul, the Lord speaks silently to the prophet's heart, confirming that this tall stranger is the one chosen to rule. The word used for rule carried a sense of firm authority and restraint. God's quiet prompt showed Samuel that His promise was being fulfilled right before his eyes.

Saul walks up to Samuel near the town gate and asks him where the seer's house is. Saul does not realize that he is talking directly to the great prophet he has been seeking. Samuel's plain dress and humble manner concealed his prominence from a stranger's eyes.

Samuel reveals that he is the seer and warmly invites Saul to walk ahead of him up to the high place to share in the sacrificial meal. He promises to send Saul on his way the next morning and to tell him everything that is on his mind. By asking Saul to walk ahead, the elder prophet pays honor to the young man who will soon lead the nation.

Before Saul can even ask about his errand, Samuel tells him that the lost donkeys have already been found. He then drops a startling hint, asking whom all Israel's desire belongs to if not to Saul and his family. This supernatural knowledge proved Samuel was a true prophet, while hinting at the royal crown awaiting Saul.

Saul responds with genuine shock, pointing out that he belongs to Benjamin, the smallest tribe in Israel, and that his family is insignificant within it. The tribe had been nearly wiped out in a civil war generations earlier and remained very small. Saul's modest reaction shows a healthy humility before the responsibilities of leadership.

Samuel leads Saul and his servant into the dining hall and seats them at the head of the table in the place of highest honor. There were about thirty guests gathered, representing the leading elders and citizens of the town. Placing a weary stranger and his servant at the seat of honor was a clear public signal that God had high plans for Saul.

Samuel turns to the cook and orders him to bring out the special portion of meat that he had instructed him to set aside earlier. This command shows that Samuel had planned the entire feast in advance, expecting God's chosen guest. Everything was moving according to God's careful design.

The cook brings out the roasted leg or shoulder and sets it directly before Saul, the traditional portion reserved for an honored guest. Samuel explains that this choice piece had been kept especially for him ever since the guests were invited. Receiving the premier portion at the banquet reinforced to Saul that his arrival was no accident.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Based on the ancient Hebrew and early Eastern translations, the cook himself spoke the words in the middle of the verse, explaining to Saul how the choice portion had been set aside for him.

notes.meaning: After the feast, they come down from the high place into the town, and Samuel takes Saul up to the flat rooftop of his house to talk privately. Flat roofs were customary places in that region for cool breezes, quiet conversation, and hosting overnight guests. Samuel used this secluded time to instruct Saul on the sacred responsibilities of leading God's covenant people.

Early the next morning, just as dawn is breaking, Samuel calls up to Saul, who had slept on the rooftop, telling him it is time to prepare for departure. Saul gets up, and the two men head out of the house together. The early start set the stage for a private meeting outside the public eye.

As they reach the edge of the town, Samuel asks Saul to send his servant ahead so the two of them can be completely alone. Samuel wants Saul to stand still in quiet attention to hear the direct word of the Lord. This private parting leads directly into Saul's secret anointing as the first king of Israel.
